original_abstract: Omnidirectional scene text detection has received increasing research attention. Previous methods directly predict words or text lines of quadrilateral shapes. However, most methods neglect the significance of consistent labeling, which is important to maintain a stable training process, especially when a large amount of data are included. For the first time, we solve the problem in this paper by proposing a novel method termed Sequential-free Box Discretization (SBD). The proposed SBD first discretizes the quadrilateral box into several key edges, which contains all potential horizontal and vertical positions. In order to decode accurate vertex positions, a simple yet effective matching procedure is proposed to reconstruct the quadrilateral bounding boxes. It departs from the learning ambiguity which has a significant influence during the learning process. Exhaustive ablation studies have been conducted to quantitatively validate the effectiveness of our proposed method. More importantly, built upon SBD, we provide a detailed analysis of the impact of a collection of refinements, in the hope to inspire others to build state-of-the-art networks. Combining both SBD and these useful refinements, we achieve state-of-the-art performance on various benchmarks, including ICDAR 2015, and MLT. Our method also wins the first place in text detection task of the recent ICDAR2019 Robust Reading Challenge on Reading Chinese Text on Signboard, further demonstrating its powerful generalization ability. Code is available at this https URL.
generated_abstract: Detecting text of arbitrary shapes in natural images is challenging, yet it is essential for reliable scene text understanding. Existing detectors have established strong performance for horizontal and oriented text by directly regressing quadrilateral boundaries or segmenting text regions, while recent methods have shown that adaptive representations can describe curved instances and that joint detection and recognition are feasible. However, these representations remain poorly suited to text with arbitrary geometry, especially when instances are long, curved, or densely arranged, and often require cumbersome proposal generation or post-processing. We introduce a flexible representation that models each text instance as an ordered sequence of overlapping disks along its centerline. Each disk is characterized by its center, radius, and orientation, allowing a unified description of curved, rotated, and elongated text. A fully convolutional network predicts text regions, centerline regions, disk geometry, and orientation fields directly from the image, and these predictions are assembled into instances with lightweight geometric reconstruction. We evaluate the approach on benchmarks spanning curved, oriented, and multilingual scene text, measuring detection accuracy, robustness to shape variation, and computational efficiency.

original_abstract: Conventional cross-domain image-to-image translation or unsupervised domain adaptation methods assume that the source domain and target domain are closely related. This neglects a practical scenario where the domain discrepancy between the source and target is excessively large. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to learn domain adaptive features between the largely-gapped source and target domains with unlabeled domain bridges. Firstly, we introduce the framework of Cycle-consistency Flow Generative Adversarial Networks (CFGAN) that utilizes domain bridges to perform image-to-image translation between two distantly distributed domains. Secondly, we propose the Prototypical Adversarial Domain Adaptation (PADA) model which utilizes unlabeled bridge domains to align feature distribution between source and target with a large discrepancy. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments are conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed models.
generated_abstract: We address unsupervised domain adaptation, in which a predictive model must transfer knowledge from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target domain whose data distribution differs from that of the source. Existing research has established that deep representations can be made more transferable by exploiting unlabeled target samples, while preserving source-domain task discrimination. It has also shown that domain discrepancy can be reduced at the pixel, feature, or joint multi-layer distribution level, using statistical moment matching, adversarial objectives, or task-specific decision boundaries, and that transfer can be extended to multiple sources and partially related tasks. Important challenges remain in preventing harmful alignment, retaining class structure, handling substantial or heterogeneous shifts, and making adaptation effective without target annotations. We therefore develop a deep learning framework that jointly learns the prediction task from labeled source examples and an adaptation signal from unlabeled target examples, using task-aware representation learning and distribution comparison to guide the transfer. The approach is evaluated empirically on established cross-domain visual recognition benchmarks, including settings with different domain shifts and, where applicable, multiple source domains, using predictive accuracy and comparisons with existing adaptation strategies.

original_abstract: The revolution in computer hardware, especially in graphics processing units and tensor processing units, has enabled significant advances in computer graphics and artificial intelligence algorithms. In addition to their many beneficial applications in daily life and business, computer-generated/manipulated images and videos can be used for malicious purposes that violate security systems, privacy, and social trust. The deepfake phenomenon and its variations enable a normal user to use his or her personal computer to easily create fake videos of anybody from a short real online video. Several countermeasures have been introduced to deal with attacks using such videos. However, most of them are targeted at certain domains and are ineffective when applied to other domains or new attacks. In this paper, we introduce a capsule network that can detect various kinds of attacks, from presentation attacks using printed images and replayed videos to attacks using fake videos created using deep learning. It uses many fewer parameters than traditional convolutional neural networks with similar performance. Moreover, we explain, for the first time ever in the literature, the theory behind the application of capsule networks to the forensics problem through detailed analysis and visualization.
generated_abstract: The rapid development of face synthesis and manipulation technologies threatens the reliability of digital visual content, biometric authentication, and online information sharing. Existing research has established that manipulated faces can be detected with learned visual representations, and that performance improves when detectors exploit domain knowledge, temporal consistency, local artifacts, or complementary image cues. It has also shown that strong results on established benchmarks do not necessarily ensure robustness to compression, changes in capture conditions, cross-dataset testing, or previously unseen manipulation techniques. We address these unresolved issues through a systematic analysis of learning-based facial forgery detection. We organize existing methods according to the visual evidence they model, the architectures and supervision they use, and the assumptions made about attacks and data distributions. We further compare available datasets, manipulation types, evaluation protocols, and reported results to identify sources of performance variation and limitations in generalization. The analysis evaluates image- and video-based detectors under differing quality levels and attack conditions, examines their transferability beyond familiar data, and highlights open requirements for reliable, scalable, and attack-agnostic detection in practical settings.

original_abstract: Neural Networks trained with gradient descent are known to be susceptible to catastrophic forgetting caused by parameter shift during the training process. In the context of Neural Machine Translation (NMT) this results in poor performance on heterogeneous datasets and on sub-tasks like rare phrase translation. On the other hand, non-parametric approaches are immune to forgetting, perfectly complementing the generalization ability of NMT. However, attempts to combine non-parametric or retrieval based approaches with NMT have only been successful on narrow domains, possibly due to over-reliance on sentence level retrieval. We propose a novel n-gram level retrieval approach that relies on local phrase level similarities, allowing us to retrieve neighbors that are useful for translation even when overall sentence similarity is low. We complement this with an expressive neural network, allowing our model to extract information from the noisy retrieved context. We evaluate our semi-parametric NMT approach on a heterogeneous dataset composed of WMT, IWSLT, JRC-Acquis and OpenSubtitles, and demonstrate gains on all 4 evaluation sets. The semi-parametric nature of our approach opens the door for non-parametric domain adaptation, demonstrating strong inference-time adaptation performance on new domains without the need for any parameter updates.
generated_abstract: Neural machine translation produces fluent translations, but its adequacy remains vulnerable to domain mismatch, limited training data, rare words and phrases, long sentences, and search errors. Attention-based sequence models have removed the fixed-vector bottleneck and established strong end-to-end performance, while analysis of their challenges has shown that phrase-based systems still provide valuable lexical coverage and domain-specific translations. Subsequent advances demonstrate that combining neural models with symbolic translation scores, retrieved examples, or broader context can recover some of this missing information, although effective integration with neural decoding remains open. We address this problem with a retrieval-augmented translation model that retains access to a large parallel corpus after training. For each source sentence, a search procedure identifies similar bilingual examples; information extracted from these examples is represented alongside the source and incorporated into the neural encoder-decoder during prediction, allowing the model to reuse relevant translation patterns while generating novel material. We evaluate the approach against strong neural and phrase-based baselines on multiple language pairs and domains, measuring translation quality, robustness to rare and repeated expressions, domain transfer, and the computational cost of retrieval and decoding.

original_abstract: In line with recent advances in neural drug design and sensitivity prediction, we propose a novel architecture for interpretable prediction of anticancer compound sensitivity using a multimodal attention-based convolutional encoder. Our model is based on the three key pillars of drug sensitivity: compounds’ structure in the form of a SMILES sequence, gene expression profiles of tumors and prior knowledge on intracellular interactions from protein-protein interaction networks. We demonstrate that our multiscale convolutional attention-based encoder significantly outperforms a baseline model trained on Morgan fingerprints, a selection of encoders based on SMILES as well as previously reported state of the art for multimodal drug sensitivity prediction (R2 = 0.86 and RMSE = 0.89). Moreover, the explainability of our approach is demonstrated by a thorough analysis of the attention weights. generated_abstract: Cancer treatment selection remains difficult because the response of a particular tumour to a compound cannot be reliably inferred from its molecular state, while experimental drug screens are costly and incomplete. Prior research has established that supervised learning can predict cell-line sensitivity from genomic or transcriptomic profiles, chemical structure, and biological interaction information, and that nonlinear models, pathway or network context, multitask learning, and joint representations of cells and drugs can improve accuracy. It has also established useful benchmarks and demonstrated applications to missing-response estimation, resistance classification, and drug repurposing. However, robust prediction for unseen cell–drug pairs remains limited by heterogeneous molecular data, sparse measurements, and imperfect transfer from model systems to new biological contexts. We address this problem with a neural representation-learning framework that encodes cancer-cell molecular features and compound structure, combines their learned representations to model treatment response, and is trained on large-scale drug-screening data. We evaluate predictive accuracy, generalization across drugs and cell lines, robustness to different input features, and utility for prioritizing potentially effective treatments and novel therapeutic associations.

original_abstract: The inability to generalize beyond the distribution of a training set is at the core of practical limits of machine learning. We show that the common practice of mixing and shuffling training examples when training deep neural networks is not optimal. On the opposite, partitioning the training data into non-i.i.d. subsets can serve to guide the model to rely on reliable statistical patterns while ignoring spurious correlations in the training data. We demonstrate multiple use cases where these subsets are built using unsupervised clustering, prior knowledge, or other meta-data from existing datasets. The approach is supported by recent results on a causal view of generalization, it is simple to apply, and it demonstrably improves generalization. Applied to the task of visual question answering, we obtain state-of-the-art performance on VQA-CP. We also show improvements over data augmentation using equivalent questions on GQA. Finally, we show a small improvement when training a model simultaneously on VQA v2 and Visual Genome, treating them as two distinct environments rather than one aggregated training set.
generated_abstract: Visual Question Answering systems often achieve strong benchmark performance without adequately grounding their answers in image content, instead exploiting correlations between question language and frequent answers. This weakness becomes apparent when answer distributions change, when visually similar images require different answers, or when language-only shortcuts are removed. Existing research has established that these priors substantially inflate conventional scores and that balancing data, adversarial training, question-only modeling, and architectural constraints can improve robustness, although their effectiveness varies and visual reasoning remains difficult to measure reliably. We address the remaining problem by systematically separating information supplied by the question from information supplied by the image. Our approach uses controlled distribution shifts and complementary or counterfactual examples, together with multimodal and unimodal prediction analyses, to determine whether a model’s decision changes for the appropriate visual reason rather than merely producing a different answer. We evaluate performance under standard and bias-sensitive splits, robustness to altered answer priors, dependence on each modality, and the quality of visual grounding reflected in model predictions and explanations.

original_abstract: Biological evolution has distilled the experiences of many learners into the general learning algorithms of humans. Our novel meta reinforcement learning algorithm MetaGenRL is inspired by this process. MetaGenRL distills the experiences of many complex agents to meta-learn a low-complexity neural objective function that affects how future individuals will learn. Unlike recent meta-RL algorithms, MetaGenRL can generalize to new environments that are entirely different from those used for meta-training. In some cases, it even outperforms human-engineered RL algorithms. MetaGenRL uses off-policy second-order gradients during meta-training that greatly increase its sample efficiency.
generated_abstract: Designing reinforcement learning algorithms that learn efficiently across diverse tasks remains a major challenge. Existing research has shown that algorithmic components can themselves be learned: recurrent agents can acquire task-adaptive learning procedures, optimization rules and loss functions can be discovered from experience, and return estimates, exploration rewards, and other update choices can be adjusted to improve performance. These results establish that meta-learning can transfer not only model parameters but also aspects of the learning process, while leaving open how broadly such approaches generalize and how reliably they can produce effective algorithms beyond their training conditions. We address this question with a meta-learning framework in which an outer learner receives performance data from agents trained on a distribution of tasks and adjusts a parameterized learning procedure used by an inner reinforcement-learning agent. The procedure can exploit trajectories, rewards, predictions, and learning histories to determine updates and exploration behavior. We evaluate the resulting methods on multiple reinforcement-learning environments and task distributions, measuring learning speed, final performance, robustness to stochasticity and architectural changes, and transfer to previously unseen or out-of-distribution tasks against established learning algorithms and ablations.

original_abstract: Reed-Muller (RM) codes are among the oldest, simplest and perhaps most ubiquitous family of codes. They are used in many areas of coding theory in both electrical engineering and computer science. Yet, many of their important properties are still under investigation. This paper covers some of the recent developments regarding the weight enumerator and the capacity-achieving properties of RM codes, as well as some of the algorithmic developments. In particular, the paper discusses the recent connections established between RM codes, thresholds of Boolean functions, polarization theory, hypercontractivity, and the techniques of approximating low weight codewords using lower degree polynomials. It then overviews some of the algorithms with performance guarantees, as well as some of the algorithms with state-of-the-art performances in practical regimes. Finally, the paper concludes with a few open problems.
generated_abstract: Reed–Muller codes combine exceptional symmetry, strong maximum-likelihood performance, and simple algebraic construction, but it remains unclear whether their practical decoding performance can match their conjectured capacity-achieving behavior on general symmetric channels. It is known that their symmetry yields capacity on erasure channels under optimal decoding, that capacity is attained in certain extreme-rate regimes for errors and erasures, and that polarization of the common Reed–Muller and polar transform provides a closely related capacity-achieving code without proving that the Reed–Muller ordering itself is optimal. Existing recursive, parity-check, and projection-based decoders also approach maximum-likelihood performance at short block lengths, although their behavior away from these regimes is unresolved. We address this gap by combining structural analysis of Reed–Muller generator and parity-check representations with numerical experiments over noisy binary-input channels, using finite-length estimates of reliability and decoding thresholds rather than assuming optimal decoding. We evaluate block-error and bit-error performance across block lengths, rates, and channel conditions, and compare the resulting behavior with polar codes, maximum-likelihood benchmarks, and established low-complexity Reed–Muller decoders. Our results characterize how closely practical decoding follows the predicted polarization and capacity trends.

original_abstract: To ensure pedestrian friendly streets in the era of automated vehicles, reassessment of current policies, practices, design, rules and regulations of urban areas is of importance. This study investigates pedestrian crossing behaviour, as an important element of urban dynamics that is expected to be affected by the presence of automated vehicles. For this purpose, an interpretable machine learning framework is proposed to explore factors affecting pedestrians' wait time before crossing mid-block crosswalks in the presence of automated vehicles. To collect rich behavioural data, we developed a dynamic and immersive virtual reality experiment, with 180 participants from a heterogeneous population in 4 different locations in the Greater Toronto Area (GTA). Pedestrian wait time behaviour is then analyzed using a data-driven Cox Proportional Hazards (CPH) model, in which the linear combination of the covariates is replaced by a flexible non-linear deep neural network. The proposed model achieved a 5% improvement in goodness of fit, but more importantly, enabled us to incorporate a richer set of covariates. A game theoretic based interpretability method is used to understand the contribution of different covariates to the time pedestrians wait before crossing. Results show that the presence of automated vehicles on roads, wider lane widths, high density on roads, limited sight distance, and lack of walking habits are the main contributing factors to longer wait times. Our study suggested that, to move towards pedestrian-friendly urban areas, national level educational programs for children, enhanced safety measures for seniors, promotion of active modes of transportation, and revised traffic rules and regulations should be considered.
generated_abstract:
Safe and efficient interaction between pedestrians and automated vehicles requires predicting when pedestrians will cross and understanding the factors behind their decisions. Existing evidence shows that crossing depends on time to collision, vehicle speed and size, available gaps, pedestrian motion, traffic signals, environmental context, and observable vehicle behavior. Nonverbal attention and explicit external messages can improve coordination, while trust and perceived safety shape responses to automated vehicles. Previous behavioral models and neural networks have demonstrated useful predictive performance, but flexible learning systems can obscure behavioral mechanisms, produce unstable local effects, and offer limited guidance for vehicle or infrastructure design.

We address this gap by learning pedestrian crossing decisions from controlled behavioral observations, including immersive interactive scenarios, using a nonlinear neural choice model that represents interactions among pedestrian, vehicle, roadway, and communication features. We complement prediction with systematic post-estimation analysis of feature contributions and response profiles, examining whether the learned relationships are behaviorally plausible and sufficiently stable for interpretation. The framework is evaluated through predictive accuracy and calibration, comparisons with conventional statistical and machine-learning baselines, robustness across observations or model fits, and the consistency and practical meaning of the inferred effects.

original_abstract: Training neural networks is traditionally done by providing a sequence of random mini-batches sampled uniformly from the entire training data. In this work, we analyze the effect of curriculum learning, which involves the non-uniform sampling of mini-batches, on the training of deep networks, and specifically CNNs trained for image recognition. To employ curriculum learning, the training algorithm must resolve 2 problems: (i) sort the training examples by difficulty; (ii) compute a series of mini-batches that exhibit an increasing level of difficulty. We address challenge (i) using two methods: transfer learning from some competitive ``teacher" network, and bootstrapping. In our empirical evaluation, both methods show similar benefits in terms of increased learning speed and improved final performance on test data. We address challenge (ii) by investigating different pacing functions to guide the sampling. The empirical investigation includes a variety of network architectures, using images from CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and subsets of ImageNet. We conclude with a novel theoretical analysis of curriculum learning, where we show how it effectively modifies the optimization landscape. We then define the concept of an ideal curriculum, and show that under mild conditions it does not change the corresponding global minimum of the optimization function.
generated_abstract: Training deep neural networks efficiently and reliably remains difficult, particularly when examples vary in difficulty, labels are noisy, and the learner must handle complex tasks or large datasets. Deep architectures and end-to-end systems have achieved strong results across vision, speech, language, and program evaluation, while curriculum-based training has been shown to accelerate optimization and improve robustness. However, deciding which examples to present, in what order, and with what emphasis is still often dependent on hand-designed rules or task-specific knowledge. We address this problem by treating curriculum construction as an adaptive teaching process. A learned teacher observes feedback from a student network during training and uses a sequential decision-making model to select or weight training data, thereby adapting the syllabus to the student’s changing state rather than fixing it in advance. We evaluate this approach across neural network architectures and learning tasks, measuring predictive performance, convergence speed, data and iteration efficiency, and robustness under challenging training conditions. The results assess whether learned curricula provide consistent benefits over conventional sampling and manually specified schedules.

original_abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks fostered a newfound interest in generative models, resulting in a swelling wave of new works that new-coming researchers may find formidable to surf. In this paper, we intend to help those researchers, by splitting that incoming wave into six "fronts": Architectural Contributions, Conditional Techniques, Normalization and Constraint Contributions, Loss Functions, Image-to-image Translations, and Validation Metrics. The division in fronts organizes literature into approachable blocks, ultimately communicating to the reader how the area is evolving. Previous surveys in the area, which this works also tabulates, focus on a few of those fronts, leaving a gap that we propose to fill with a more integrated, comprehensive overview. Here, instead of an exhaustive survey, we opt for a straightforward review: our target is to be an entry point to this vast literature, and also to be able to update experienced researchers to the newest techniques.
generated_abstract: Generating photorealistic images that are both diverse and free of synthesis artifacts remains a central challenge in generative modeling. Adversarial learning has already made it possible to produce convincing images at high resolution, while progressively refined architectures, conditional inputs, large-scale training, and style-based latent representations have improved stability, controllability, fidelity, and the separation of semantic attributes from stochastic detail. Nevertheless, characteristic artifacts persist, the mapping from latent variables to images can be poorly behaved, and commonly used measures do not fully reflect perceptual quality or interpolation smoothness. We address these limitations through an ablation-driven redesign of a style-modulated convolutional generator. The method removes signal-dependent normalization effects by modulating and demodulating convolutional weights, replaces progressive growing with a revised multi-resolution design, and regularizes the generator’s image-space Jacobian so that nearby latent codes produce consistently sized perceptual changes. We evaluate the resulting models on diverse high-resolution face and natural-image datasets, measuring fidelity, diversity, artifact prevalence, latent-space disentanglement, and interpolation quality with distributional metrics, controlled experiments, and human perceptual judgments.

original_abstract: Local differential privacy (LDP) can provide each user with strong privacy guarantees under untrusted data curators while ensuring accurate statistics derived from privatized data. Due to its powerfulness, LDP has been widely adopted to protect privacy in various tasks (e.g., heavy hitters discovery, probability estimation) and systems (e.g., Google Chrome, Apple iOS). Although ${\epsilon}$-LDP has been proposed for many years, the more general notion of $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP has only been studied in very few papers, which mainly consider mean estimation for numeric data. Besides, prior solutions achieve $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP by leveraging Gaussian mechanism, which leads to low accuracy of the aggregated results. In this paper, we propose novel mechanisms that achieve $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP with high utility in data analytics and machine learning. Specifically, we first design $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP algorithms for collecting multi-dimensional numeric data, which can ensure higher accuracy than the optimal Gaussian mechanism while guaranteeing strong privacy for each user. Then, we investigate different local protocols for categorical attributes under $({\epsilon}, {\delta})$-LDP. Furthermore, we conduct theoretical analysis on the error bound and variance of the proposed algorithms. Experimental results on real and synthetic datasets demonstrate the high data utility of our proposed algorithms on both simple data statistics and complex machine learning models.
generated_abstract: Protecting sensitive user information while retaining useful statistical and predictive power remains a central challenge in data-driven applications. Local differential privacy provides protection at the user device, so the data collector receives only randomized information, while prior work has established mechanisms and accuracy guarantees for numerical, categorical, marginal, key-value, and distributional estimation. It has also characterized fundamental privacy–utility limits for several estimation problems and demonstrated that centrally private neural networks can be trained on sensitive data. However, practical learning of complex, high-dimensional, nonconvex models when privacy must be enforced locally remains insufficiently understood. We address this gap by developing a locally private training procedure for neural networks based on iterative stochastic optimization: user contributions are bounded and randomized before aggregation, and the resulting noisy updates are used to fit the model without exposing individual records to the learner. We study the resulting privacy, optimization, and utility behavior and evaluate the approach on representative real-world datasets and learning tasks. The experiments examine predictive accuracy, convergence, computational and communication costs, and the tradeoff between privacy protection and model quality against nonprivate and existing private alternatives.

original_abstract: We investigate the combination of actor-critic reinforcement learning algorithms with uniform large-scale experience replay and propose solutions for two challenges: (a) efficient actor-critic learning with experience replay (b) stability of very off-policy learning. We employ those insights to accelerate hyper-parameter sweeps in which all participating agents run concurrently and share their experience via a common replay module. To this end we analyze the bias-variance tradeoffs in V-trace, a form of importance sampling for actor-critic methods. Based on our analysis, we then argue for mixing experience sampled from replay with on-policy experience, and propose a new trust region scheme that scales effectively to data distributions where V-trace becomes unstable. We provide extensive empirical validation of the proposed solution. We further show the benefits of this setup by demonstrating state-of-the-art data efficiency on Atari among agents trained up until 200M environment frames.
generated_abstract: Deep reinforcement learning has made progress in learning control directly from high-dimensional observations, yet reliable performance across diverse tasks remains difficult. Atari games provide a demanding test: agents can learn strong policies from pixels, and distributed acting, replay, off-policy learning, and improved value and policy estimation can accelerate training. Nevertheless, performance remains uneven, particularly on games requiring directed exploration, long horizons, or sparse rewards, and agents have not matched human performance across the benchmark. We introduce an agent designed to address these limitations by combining task rewards with intrinsic signals based on novelty. It maintains episodic memory to reward visits to unfamiliar states and a longer-term estimate of persistent novelty, while a recurrent neural policy handles partial observability. A learned controller selects among policies with different exploration and discounting behaviors, and distributed actors supply experience for off-policy updates. We evaluate the resulting system on all 57 Atari 2600 games, measuring learning efficiency and final performance against human and established agent baselines. The system achieves robust performance on exploration-intensive tasks and establishes a new level of generality for a single deep reinforcement learning agent.

original_abstract: The design of deep graph models still remains to be investigated and the crucial part is how to explore and exploit the knowledge from different hops of neighbors in an efficient way. In this paper, we propose a novel RNN-like deep graph neural network architecture by incorporating AdaBoost into the computation of network; and the proposed graph convolutional network called AdaGCN~(AdaBoosting Graph Convolutional Network) has the ability to efficiently extract knowledge from high-order neighbors and integrate knowledge from different hops of neighbors into the network in an AdaBoost way. We also present the architectural difference between AdaGCN and existing graph convolutional methods to show the benefits of our proposal. Finally, extensive experiments demonstrate the state-of-the-art prediction performance and the computational advantage of our approach AdaGCN.
generated_abstract: Graph neural networks have become effective tools for learning on graph-structured data, but most graph convolutional models remain shallow. Increasing depth can enlarge the receptive field and capture long-range dependencies, yet often causes optimization difficulties, excessive smoothing, and the loss of discriminative information. Existing research has established that neighborhood aggregation provides an efficient and scalable generalization of convolution, performs strongly in semi-supervised node classification, and can exploit multi-scale information through adaptive propagation or connections across layers. It has also revealed fundamental limits in the expressive power of common aggregation schemes and the tendency of repeated propagation to make node representations indistinguishable. We investigate whether graph convolutional networks can be made substantially deeper while retaining useful representations. Our approach constructs deep architectures using residual and dense skip connections, expanded receptive fields through dilated neighborhood aggregation, and flexible feature-combination operators that preserve information across propagation scales. We analyze the resulting architectures and compare their optimization and representation behavior with shallower and existing deep models. Experiments evaluate node classification, graph classification, and three-dimensional point-cloud semantic segmentation, demonstrating the practical value of deep graph convolution.

original_abstract: This paper seeks to answer a simple but fundamental question: what role can non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) play in massive multi-in multi-out (MIMO)? It is well established that power-domain NOMA schemes can outperform conventional orthogonal multiple access schemes in cellular networks. However, this fact does not imply that NOMA is the most efficient way to communicate in massive MIMO setups, where the base stations have many more antennas than there are users in the cell. These setups are becoming the norm in future networks and are usually studied by assuming spatial multiplexing of the users using linear multi-user beamforming. To answer the above-mentioned question, we analyze and compare the performance achieved by NOMA and multi-user beamforming in both non-line-of-sight and line-of-sight scenarios. We reveal that the latter scheme gives the highest average sum rate in massive MIMO setups. We also identify specific cases where NOMA is the better choice in massive MIMO and explain how NOMA plays an essential role in creating a hybrid of NOMA and multi-user beamforming that is shown to perform better than two standalone schemes do.
generated_abstract: Nonorthogonal multiple access (NOMA) must be made compatible with scalable multiuser MIMO architectures while retaining their spectral-efficiency, connectivity, and implementation advantages. Existing results establish that massive MIMO can focus energy and separate users through excess antennas, that favorable propagation is central but is not guaranteed in correlated or line-of-sight environments, and that channel hardening cannot always support conventional rate bounds or eliminate downlink training. They also show that NOMA can multiplex users through superposition coding and successive interference cancellation, but its gains depend on user ordering, channel-state acquisition, pilot design, beamforming, power allocation, and the propagation regime; in sufficiently rich multiuser settings, spatial multiplexing may be preferable. We address the remaining design and performance question by formulating a multiuser downlink model that combines large-array beamforming with power-domain superposition and successive decoding, while accounting for practical channel knowledge and propagation conditions. We derive tractable achievable-rate characterizations and use numerical evaluation to examine the effects of array size, user grouping, power allocation, feedback or training, and channel conditions, comparing the resulting NOMA operation with orthogonal and spatial-multiplexing alternatives.

original_abstract: In [1, 2], we have explored the theoretical aspects of feature extraction optimization processes for solving largescale problems and overcoming machine learning limitations. Majority of optimization algorithms that have been introduced in [1, 2] guarantee the optimal performance of supervised learning, given offline and discrete data, to deal with curse of dimensionality (CoD) problem. These algorithms, however, are not tailored for solving emerging learning problems. One of the important issues caused by online data is lack of sufficient samples per class. Further, traditional machine learning algorithms cannot achieve accurate training based on limited distributed data, as data has proliferated and dispersed significantly. Machine learning employs a strict model or embedded engine to train and predict which still fails to learn unseen classes and sufficiently use online data. In this chapter, we introduce these challenges elaborately. We further investigate Meta-Learning (MTL) algorithm, and their application and promises to solve the emerging problems by answering how autonomous agents can learn to learn?.
generated_abstract: We address the problem of learning new concepts and tasks from only a handful of labeled examples, where conventional supervised training tends to overfit and adaptation can be slow or unreliable. Prior research has established that experience gathered across many related tasks can provide a useful inductive bias for rapid learning, through learned comparison spaces, class prototypes, gradient-based initialization, task-specific transformations, synthetic examples, and distributions over plausible models. Nevertheless, few-shot systems remain vulnerable to ambiguity, architectural and optimization sensitivity, and shifts in the structure or distribution of tasks encountered at deployment. We develop a meta-learning approach that learns from episodically constructed tasks, using shared representations and an adaptation mechanism trained to convert sparse support data into predictions for unseen queries. The formulation is designed to separate transferable knowledge from information that must be inferred for each new task, while allowing uncertainty or task variation to be represented rather than forcing a single fixed solution. We evaluate the method on standard few-shot classification settings, including different numbers of examples per class and previously unseen categories, and compare accuracy, adaptation behavior, computational demands, and generalization under challenging task or domain changes.

original_abstract: Edge computing is an emerging concept based on distributing computing, storage, and control services closer to end network nodes. Edge computing lies at the heart of the fifth generation (5G) wireless systems and beyond. While current state-of-the-art networks communicate, compute, and process data in a centralized manner (at the cloud), for latency and compute-centric applications, both radio access and computational resources must be brought closer to the edge, harnessing the availability of computing and storage-enabled small cell base stations in proximity to the end devices. Furthermore, the network infrastructure must enable a distributed edge decision-making service that learns to adapt to the network dynamics with minimal latency and optimize network deployment and operation accordingly. This article will provide a fresh look to the concept of edge computing by first discussing the applications that the network edge must provide, with a special emphasis on the ensuing challenges in enabling ultra-reliable and low-latency edge computing services for mission-critical applications such as virtual reality (VR), vehicle-to-everything (V2X), edge artificial intelligence (AI), and so forth. Furthermore, several case studies where the edge is key are explored followed by insights and prospect for future work.
generated_abstract: Ultra-reliable and low-latency services at the wireless edge must support computation-intensive applications despite limited device energy, fluctuating wireless channels, user mobility, and constrained edge resources. Average throughput, delay, and queue-length measures are inadequate when rare deadline violations determine service quality. Existing research has established mobile edge computing as a means of reducing device burden and latency, and has developed joint offloading and resource-allocation methods based on stochastic control. It has also shown how tail constraints can be expressed probabilistically using extreme-value analysis, while dynamic association, mobility management, and distributed edge learning can exploit local information and multiple decision timescales. However, a scalable framework that captures the coupled effects of communication, computation, mobility, and reliability remains open. We address this gap by constructing a stochastic network model with evolving queues, wireless states, user–server associations, and computational workloads, and by designing a distributed, timescale-separated optimization and control procedure that enforces probabilistic service constraints rather than optimizing averages alone. We evaluate its latency, reliability, energy or power consumption, resource utilization, and scalability under varying traffic, mobility, channel, and computation conditions, comparing performance with conventional policies.

original_abstract: Automatic Post-Editing (APE) aims to correct systematic errors in a machine translated text. This is primarily useful when the machine translation (MT) system is not accessible for improvement, leaving APE as a viable option to improve translation quality as a downstream task - which is the focus of this thesis. This field has received less attention compared to MT due to several reasons, which include: the limited availability of data to perform a sound research, contrasting views reported by different researchers about the effectiveness of APE, and limited attention from the industry to use APE in current production pipelines. In this thesis, we perform a thorough investigation of APE as a downstream task in order to: i) understand its potential to improve translation quality; ii) advance the core technology - starting from classical methods to recent deep-learning based solutions; iii) cope with limited and sparse data; iv) better leverage multiple input sources; v) mitigate the task-specific problem of over-correction; vi) enhance neural decoding to leverage external knowledge; and vii) establish an online learning framework to handle data diversity in real-time. All the above contributions are discussed across several chapters, and most of them are evaluated in the APE shared task organized each year at the Conference on Machine Translation. Our efforts in improving the technology resulted in the best system at the 2017 APE shared task, and our work on online learning received a distinguished paper award at the Italian Conference on Computational Linguistics. Overall, outcomes and findings of our work have boost interest among researchers and attracted industries to examine this technology to solve real-word problems.
generated_abstract: Automatic post-editing seeks to improve machine-translated text without modifying the underlying translation system, thereby reducing human editing effort and correcting recurrent errors while preserving adequate output. Previous research has shown that statistical, phrase-based, and neural post-editing systems can outperform unedited machine translation, particularly when they exploit both the source sentence and the machine-translated hypothesis. Neural sequence-to-sequence models with attention, model combinations, quality-estimation features, synthetic training data, and reranking have further improved automatic scores, while online adaptation has demonstrated that post-edits can also be used to update translation models. Nevertheless, reliable correction remains difficult when training data are scarce, the initial translation is already strong, or the post-editor overcorrects fluent and faithful content. We address these limitations with a neural conditional generation framework that represents the source and machine translation jointly, learns from available human post-edits supplemented by automatically constructed examples, and combines candidate generation with evidence about translation quality to favor conservative corrections. We evaluate the approach on established automatic post-editing benchmarks, comparing it with unedited machine translation and competitive statistical and neural systems using automatic metrics and, where available, human judgments.

original_abstract: We consider a variant of the classic Ski Rental online algorithm with applications to machine learning. In our variant, we allow the skier access to a black-box machine-learning algorithm that provides an estimate of the probability that there will be at most a threshold number of ski-days. We derive a class of optimal randomized algorithms to determine the strategy that minimizes the worst-case expected competitive ratio for the skier given a prediction from the machine learning algorithm,and analyze the performance and robustness of these algorithms.
generated_abstract: Online decision-making must cope with uncertainty while exploiting regularities in data that can predict future events. Existing results have shown that machine-learned predictions can improve classical online algorithms, including caching, ski rental, and scheduling, while preserving guarantees when predictions are inaccurate. Related work has also connected prediction quality to advertising revenue and demonstrated that average-case assumptions can yield behavior different from worst-case analysis. However, a general understanding of how predictive information should be incorporated, and how its benefits trade off against robustness, remains incomplete. We develop an online optimization framework that treats predictions as potentially noisy advice and combines them with a conservative decision rule derived from worst-case analysis. Using explicit error measures and distributional assumptions, we derive performance guarantees that improve as prediction accuracy increases while remaining bounded when predictions are poor. We study the resulting tradeoffs through competitive and average-case analyses for representative online decision problems, and evaluate the approach experimentally using simulated and real-world data. The evaluation examines performance across prediction accuracies, input distributions, and baseline strategies, including the cost of relying directly on unverified forecasts.

original_abstract: While deep learning (DL)-based networked systems have shown great potential in various applications, a key drawback is that Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in DL are blackboxes and nontransparent for network operators. The lack of interpretability makes DL-based networked systems challenging to operate and troubleshoot, which further prevents DL-based networked systems from deploying in practice. In this paper, we propose TranSys, a novel framework to explain DL-based networked systems for practical deployment. Transys categorizes current DL-based networked systems and introduces different explanation methods based on decision tree and hypergraph to effectively explain DL-based networked systems. TranSys can explain the DNN policies in the form of decision trees and highlight critical components based on analysis over hypergraph. We evaluate TranSys over several typical DL-based networked systems and demonstrate that Transys can provide human-readable explanations for network operators. We also present three use cases of Transys, which could (i) help network operators troubleshoot DL-based networked systems, (ii) improve the decision latency and resource consumption of DL-based networked systems by ~10x on different metrics, and (iii) provide suggestions on daily operations for network operators when incidences occur.
generated_abstract: Machine learning is increasingly used to model and control communication networks, yet the opacity of learned decision makers limits trust, diagnosis, and safe deployment. Existing work has shown that neural models can accurately generalize across network topologies, traffic conditions, routing schemes, and operational workloads, while interpretability methods can associate internal representations with concepts, assign importance to input features, identify influential graph structures, and reveal anomalous reinforcement-learning behavior. Formal analysis can additionally check whether learned policies satisfy specified properties, but these techniques remain dependent on the model, task, and explanation sought, leaving a need for systematic understanding of what network models have learned and why they act as they do. We address this gap through a black-box analysis framework that probes trained models with controlled variations of network states, inputs, and structural conditions, and examines the resulting predictions or actions using feature-, structure-, and behavior-level explanations. The framework is evaluated on learned networking models and representative decision-making tasks, assessing whether the resulting analyses are faithful, stable, and useful for uncovering salient dependencies, unexpected behavior, and limitations relevant to network operation.

original_abstract: This paper proposes the first model-free Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework to synthesise policies for unknown, and continuous-state Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), such that a given linear temporal property is satisfied. We convert the given property into a Limit Deterministic Buchi Automaton (LDBA), namely a finite-state machine expressing the property. Exploiting the structure of the LDBA, we shape a synchronous reward function on-the-fly, so that an RL algorithm can synthesise a policy resulting in traces that probabilistically satisfy the linear temporal property. This probability (certificate) is also calculated in parallel with policy learning when the state space of the MDP is finite: as such, the RL algorithm produces a policy that is certified with respect to the property. Under the assumption of finite state space, theoretical guarantees are provided on the convergence of the RL algorithm to an optimal policy, maximising the above probability. We also show that our method produces ''best available'' control policies when the logical property cannot be satisfied. In the general case of a continuous state space, we propose a neural network architecture for RL and we empirically show that the algorithm finds satisfying policies, if there exist such policies. The performance of the proposed framework is evaluated via a set of numerical examples and benchmarks, where we observe an improvement of one order of magnitude in the number of iterations required for the policy synthesis, compared to existing approaches whenever available.
generated_abstract: We address the synthesis of control policies for agents operating in stochastic, partially known, and potentially heterogeneous environments, where performance must be learned while temporal-logic safety and task requirements are respected throughout exploration. Existing results show that unknown Markov decision processes can be learned with probabilistic performance guarantees, and that automata-based representations can convert temporal specifications into objectives for model-based or model-free reinforcement learning. They also show that permissive safe strategies and verification-preserving model updates can protect execution under a fixed model or a collection of candidate models. Important challenges remain in combining these ideas without requiring a complete environmental model or eliminating useful exploration. We develop a learning framework that synchronizes the specification with an incrementally constructed decision model, uses transition observations to update both the policy and the set of admissible behaviors, and filters exploration through actions whose safety can be established across the currently supported models. The resulting procedure balances restriction and information gathering while optimizing the learned task objective. We evaluate safety preservation, specification satisfaction, policy quality, learning efficiency, and computational scalability in numerical control and motion-planning experiments.

original_abstract: Many inferential and learning tasks can be accomplished efficiently by means of distributed optimization algorithms where the network topology plays a critical role in driving the local interactions among neighboring agents. There is a large body of literature examining the effect of the graph structure on the performance of optimization strategies. In this article, we examine the inverse problem and consider the reverse question: How much information does observing the behavior at the nodes convey about the underlying network structure used for optimization? Over large-scale networks, the difficulty of addressing such inverse questions (or problems) is compounded by the fact that usually only a limited portion of nodes can be probed, giving rise to a second important question: Despite the presence of several unobserved nodes, are partial and local observations still sufficient to discover the graph linking the probed nodes? The article surveys recent advances on this inverse learning problem and related questions. Examples of applications are provided to illustrate how the interplay between graph learning and distributed optimization arises in practice, e.g., in cognitive engineered systems such as distributed detection, or in other real-world problems such as the mechanism of opinion formation over social networks and the mechanism of coordination in biological networks. A unifying framework for examining the reconstruction error will be described, which allows to devise and examine various estimation strategies enabling successful graph learning. The relevance of specific network attributes, such as sparsity versus density of connections, and node degree concentration, is discussed in relation to the topology inference goal. It is shown how universal (i.e., data-driven) clustering algorithms can be exploited to solve the graph learning problem.
generated_abstract: We study the problem of recovering the interaction structure among a set of observable agents when the network is large, only a fraction of its agents can be monitored, and observations consist of indirect outputs generated by a diffusion or adaptive learning process. This setting is intrinsically underdetermined: unobserved agents and latent interactions obscure the topology, while the observable subnetwork may have arbitrary structure. Existing results have shown that local tomography can nevertheless be consistent in large networks under suitable stochastic models for the latent portion, and that concentration of node degrees, rather than sparsity alone, can create an identifiability gap between interacting and non-interacting agents. They have also established recovery through temporal statistics and clustering under several symmetry and stability conditions. We address the remaining question of how these principles extend across observation regimes and interaction rules by modeling the hidden network probabilistically, extracting estimators from successive observed states and their temporal dependence, and analyzing their concentration and separability as the network grows. We evaluate recovery accuracy, robustness to dense connectivity and asymmetric interactions, and finite-size performance through controlled numerical experiments.

original_abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) has recently led to many breakthroughs on a range of complex control tasks. However, the agent's decision-making process is generally not transparent. The lack of interpretability hinders the applicability of RL in safety-critical scenarios. While several methods have attempted to interpret vision-based RL, most come without detailed explanation for the agent's behaviour. In this paper, we propose a self-supervised interpretable framework, which can discover causal features to enable easy interpretation of RL agents even for non-experts. Specifically, a self-supervised interpretable network (SSINet) is employed to produce fine-grained attention masks for highlighting task-relevant information, which constitutes most evidence for the agent's decisions. We verify and evaluate our method on several Atari 2600 games as well as Duckietown, which is a challenging self-driving car simulator environment. The results show that our method renders causal explanations and empirical evidences about how the agent makes decisions and why the agent performs well or badly, especially when transferred to novel scenes. Overall, our method provides valuable insight into the internal decision-making process of vision-based RL. In addition, our method does not use any external labelled data, and thus demonstrates the possibility to learn high-quality mask through a self-supervised manner, which may shed light on new paradigms for label-free vision learning such as self-supervised segmentation and detection.
generated_abstract: Deep reinforcement learning agents can achieve high performance from visual observations, yet their policies remain difficult to understand, verify, and debug. This opacity limits confidence in their decisions and makes it unclear whether success depends on meaningful game features or accidental correlations in training trajectories. Existing research has shown that attention mechanisms and saliency analyses can expose regions and features associated with action selection, reveal recurring strategies, track changes during learning, and support human understanding. It has also demonstrated that interpretable attention-based agents can approach competitive performance. However, visual explanations may be heuristic, architectures may learn shallow or overfitted representations, and the relationship between highlighted information and the policy’s actual decision process remains insufficiently established. We address this gap with a trainable visual reinforcement-learning model that produces spatially localized importance information while learning its policy from interaction, and with analyses that test explanations by altering or withholding the indicated observations. We evaluate the approach in visual control environments, measuring task performance alongside explanation fidelity, behavioral consistency, robustness to perturbations, and the usefulness of the resulting visualizations for diagnosing agent strategies.

original_abstract: Concolic testing is a test generation technique which works effectively by integrating random testing generation and symbolic execution. Existing concolic testing engines focus on numeric programs. Heap-manipulating programs make extensive use of complex heap objects like trees and lists. Testing such programs is challenging due to multiple reasons. Firstly, test inputs for such program are required to satisfy non-trivial constraints which must be specified precisely. Secondly, precisely encoding and solving path conditions in such programs are challenging and often expensive. In this work, we propose the first concolic testing engine called CSF for heap-manipulating programs based on separation logic. CSF effectively combines specification-based testing and concolic execution for test input generation. It is evaluated on a set of challenging heap-manipulating programs. The results show that CSF generates valid test inputs with high coverage efficiently. Furthermore, we show that CSF can be potentially used in combination with precondition inference tools to reduce the user effort.
generated_abstract: Automated testing and verification of heap-manipulating programs remain difficult when inputs are unbounded, richly structured objects whose legal construction and internal shape determine which paths are reachable. Existing techniques have shown that separation-logic descriptions can represent heap structure precisely, avoid many invalid inputs, and support compositional symbolic execution, while shape, size, and bag information can establish useful properties of data structures. They have also shown that fuzzing and search-based generation scale to broad exploration, and that selective symbolic execution can cross complex path constraints. Nevertheless, no single method reliably combines valid construction through program interfaces, deep structural reachability, and efficient exploration without incurring path explosion. We address this gap with an analysis that represents inputs and intermediate heaps using compositional, user-defined shape constraints enriched with sizes and value multisets, derives path conditions by symbolic execution, and turns remaining construction and exploration choices into guided search. The resulting procedure alternates concrete execution with constraint solving to refine structure and control-flow decisions. We evaluate it on programs and libraries manipulating complex data structures, measuring validity, coverage, scalability, and deep-path discovery.

original_abstract: Prior work on controllable text generation usually assumes that the controlled attribute can take on one of a small set of values known a priori. In this work, we propose a novel task, where the syntax of a generated sentence is controlled rather by a sentential exemplar. To evaluate quantitatively with standard metrics, we create a novel dataset with human annotations. We also develop a variational model with a neural module specifically designed for capturing syntactic knowledge and several multitask training objectives to promote disentangled representation learning. Empirically, the proposed model is observed to achieve improvements over baselines and learn to capture desirable characteristics.
generated_abstract: Neural text generation systems must produce fluent language while preserving content, maintaining coherence over long spans, and allowing diversity and explicit control. Existing neural decoders generate locally and often yield generic or repetitive outputs, whereas latent-variable, hierarchical, disentangled, prototype-based, exemplar-based, and template-based formulations have shown that sentence-level structure can improve diversity, coherence, interpretability, and controllability. Yet these properties are difficult to obtain simultaneously, and the relationship between latent representations and observable generation behavior remains incompletely understood. We address this gap with a neural latent-variable generation framework that encodes text into global representations, separates content from surface realization where possible, and uses an autoregressive decoder conditioned on those representations. Training combines reconstruction with objectives that encourage informative, distinct, and controllable codes, while decoding supports generation, transformation, and editing from the same representation space. We evaluate the approach on language modeling and conditional generation tasks, measuring fluency, diversity, coherence, content preservation, control accuracy, and interpretability through automatic metrics, human judgments, and qualitative analysis.

original_abstract: Hyperspectral images (HSI) provide rich spectral information that contributed to the successful performance improvement of numerous computer vision tasks. However, it can only be achieved at the expense of images' spatial resolution. Hyperspectral image super-resolution (HSI-SR) addresses this problem by fusing low resolution (LR) HSI with multispectral image (MSI) carrying much higher spatial resolution (HR). All existing HSI-SR approaches require the LR HSI and HR MSI to be well registered and the reconstruction accuracy of the HR HSI relies heavily on the registration accuracy of different modalities. This paper exploits the uncharted problem domain of HSI-SR without the requirement of multi-modality registration. Given the unregistered LR HSI and HR MSI with overlapped regions, we design a unique unsupervised learning structure linking the two unregistered modalities by projecting them into the same statistical space through the same encoder. The mutual information (MI) is further adopted to capture the non-linear statistical dependencies between the representations from two modalities (carrying spatial information) and their raw inputs. By maximizing the MI, spatial correlations between different modalities can be well characterized to further reduce the spectral distortion. A collaborative $l_{2,1}$ norm is employed as the reconstruction error instead of the more common $l_2$ norm, so that individual pixels can be recovered as accurately as possible. With this design, the network allows to extract correlated spectral and spatial information from unregistered images that better preserves the spectral information. The proposed method is referred to as unregistered and unsupervised mutual Dirichlet Net ($u^2$-MDN). Extensive experimental results using benchmark HSI datasets demonstrate the superior performance of $u^2$-MDN as compared to the state-of-the-art.
generated_abstract: Hyperspectral imaging provides detailed spectral signatures for material analysis, but sensor limitations generally require a trade-off between spatial and spectral resolution. Hyperspectral super-resolution therefore seeks to reconstruct a spatially detailed hyperspectral image by combining a spatially coarse hyperspectral observation with a spatially finer multispectral or RGB observation. Existing research has shown that convolutional and residual networks can learn effective nonlinear mappings, while model-based, tensor, unmixing, and unsupervised formulations can impose spectral structure, preserve spatial detail, and reduce reliance on high-resolution training targets. Nevertheless, accurate reconstruction remains difficult when ground-truth data are scarce, sensor degradation processes are uncertain, or methods trained on simulated observations are applied to real scenes. We address these limitations with a data-driven spatial–spectral fusion framework that learns the relationship between the complementary observations while incorporating their degradation and consistency constraints, reducing dependence on manually designed priors and fixed sensor characteristics. We evaluate reconstruction quality, spatial enhancement, spectral fidelity, robustness to observation conditions, and computational efficiency on simulated and real datasets through quantitative comparisons and visual analysis against representative super-resolution and fusion methods.

original_abstract: This paper presents SimCLR: a simple framework for contrastive learning of visual representations. We simplify recently proposed contrastive self-supervised learning algorithms without requiring specialized architectures or a memory bank. In order to understand what enables the contrastive prediction tasks to learn useful representations, we systematically study the major components of our framework. We show that (1) composition of data augmentations plays a critical role in defining effective predictive tasks, (2) introducing a learnable nonlinear transformation between the representation and the contrastive loss substantially improves the quality of the learned representations, and (3) contrastive learning benefits from larger batch sizes and more training steps compared to supervised learning. By combining these findings, we are able to considerably outperform previous methods for self-supervised and semi-supervised learning on ImageNet. A linear classifier trained on self-supervised representations learned by SimCLR achieves 76.5% top-1 accuracy, which is a 7% relative improvement over previous state-of-the-art, matching the performance of a supervised ResNet-50. When fine-tuned on only 1% of the labels, we achieve 85.8% top-5 accuracy, outperforming AlexNet with 100X fewer labels.
generated_abstract: We study the problem of learning useful visual representations without human annotations, a prerequisite for scalable recognition and transfer. Existing self-supervised methods have shown that carefully chosen pretext tasks and instance-level discrimination can produce semantic features and substantially narrow the gap to supervised pretraining. Yet the influence of view generation, architecture, optimization, and the representation used by the learning objective remains insufficiently understood, and performance is sensitive to these choices. We develop a training framework that creates two independently augmented views of each image, encodes them with a shared convolutional network, maps the outputs through a learned nonlinear projection, and optimizes a temperature-scaled normalized objective that identifies corresponding views among many alternatives. Through systematic studies, we quantify the effects of augmentation composition, projection depth, batch size, training duration, and model capacity, showing how these factors govern representation quality. We evaluate the resulting features with frozen linear classification and transfer learning on ImageNet and downstream tasks including object detection and semantic segmentation. The results demonstrate strong performance without labels and surpass supervised pretraining in several transfer settings.

original_abstract: Existing analysis work in machine reading comprehension (MRC) is largely concerned with evaluating the capabilities of systems. However, the capabilities of datasets are not assessed for benchmarking language understanding precisely. We propose a semi-automated, ablation-based methodology for this challenge; By checking whether questions can be solved even after removing features associated with a skill requisite for language understanding, we evaluate to what degree the questions do not require the skill. Experiments on 10 datasets (e.g., CoQA, SQuAD v2.0, and RACE) with a strong baseline model show that, for example, the relative scores of a baseline model provided with content words only and with shuffled sentence words in the context are on average 89.2% and 78.5% of the original score, respectively. These results suggest that most of the questions already answered correctly by the model do not necessarily require grammatical and complex reasoning. For precise benchmarking, MRC datasets will need to take extra care in their design to ensure that questions can correctly evaluate the intended skills.
generated_abstract: Machine reading comprehension benchmarks are intended to measure whether systems understand questions and passages, yet high benchmark scores do not necessarily indicate genuine language understanding. Existing research has established large supervised datasets and strong neural readers, while also showing that performance can be inflated by lexical overlap, dataset artifacts, answerability shortcuts, and reliance on a small portion of the passage. Adversarial insertions, unanswerable questions, conversational context, paraphrase, external knowledge, and reasoning across multiple sentences expose substantial weaknesses that conventional aggregate scores conceal. We address this gap through a controlled empirical study of reading comprehension behavior, combining diagnostic data partitions with simple question-only, passage-only, and full-input baselines and targeted analyses of the reasoning skills required by individual questions. This approach separates genuine use of context from exploitation of superficial regularities and identifies which linguistic and inferential demands drive difficulty. We evaluate representative systems and datasets under standard and diagnostic conditions, comparing automatic performance with human judgments where available. The results characterize the reliability of current benchmarks and clarify the capabilities that future reading comprehension models must demonstrate.

original_abstract: Spatio-temporal action localization is a challenging yet fascinating task that aims to detect and classify human actions in video clips. In this paper, we develop a high-level video understanding module which can encode interactions between actors and objects both in space and time. In our formulation, spatio-temporal relationships are learned by performing self-attention operations on a graph structure connecting entities from consecutive clips. Noticeably, the use of graph learning is unprecedented for this task. From a computational point of view, the proposed module is backbone independent by design and does not need end-to-end training. When tested on the AVA dataset, it demonstrates a 10-16% relative mAP improvement over the baseline. Further, it can outperform or bring performances comparable to state-of-the-art models which require heavy end-to-end and synchronized training on multiple GPUs. Code is publicly available at: this https URL.
generated_abstract: Recognizing and localizing human actions in video requires models that capture appearance, motion, and temporal structure across different spatial and temporal scales, while remaining practical for long and untrimmed sequences. Existing research has established that appearance from individual frames and motion from adjacent frames provide complementary evidence, that jointly learned three-dimensional representations generally outperform purely image-based processing, and that factorized, residual, multi-rate, and long-range temporal operators can improve accuracy and efficiency. It has also shown that linking local predictions into temporally coherent tubes enables action detection, although proposal generation, feature fusion, and temporal association remain challenging. We address these open issues with a learned deep spatiotemporal video model that processes visual content over time, combines complementary appearance and motion information within a unified representation, and uses temporal context to support both recognition and localization. The model is trained end to end on annotated video clips and evaluated on established action-recognition and action-detection benchmarks. We report classification and localization performance, compare against existing spatial, temporal, and three-dimensional architectures, and analyze the contributions of temporal modeling, feature fusion, and sequence-level prediction.

original_abstract: Low bit-width integer weights and activations are very important for efficient inference, especially with respect to lower power consumption. We propose Monte Carlo methods to quantize the weights and activations of pre-trained neural networks without any re-training. By performing importance sampling we obtain quantized low bit-width integer values from full-precision weights and activations. The precision, sparsity, and complexity are easily configurable by the amount of sampling performed. Our approach, called Monte Carlo Quantization (MCQ), is linear in both time and space, with the resulting quantized, sparse networks showing minimal accuracy loss when compared to the original full-precision networks. Our method either outperforms or achieves competitive results on multiple benchmarks compared to previous quantization methods that do require additional training.
generated_abstract: We address the challenge of deploying deep neural networks on resource-constrained hardware, where the storage, computation, and energy costs of high-precision parameters and intermediate values limit practical use. Previous research has established that weights, activations, gradients, and errors can be represented with binary, ternary, or other low-bitwidth values, replacing multiplications with inexpensive bit operations and substantially reducing model size. It has also shown that quantization-aware training and learned scaling or quantization parameters can preserve accuracy across several image-classification tasks, although accuracy gaps, training complexity, and the need for floating-point computation remain important limitations. We develop a quantized training framework that represents network quantities with constrained integer values while retaining trainable underlying parameters and differentiable approximations for optimization.
